name: Streets each depot is nearest to
returns: a list of two whole numbers
brief:
Two delivery firms share a town map, `grid`, a list of equal-length strings. `#` is a building, `.` is a street cell, `A` is a depot of the first firm and `B` a depot of the second. People walk to the cell above, below, left or right, through streets and depots. A street cell belongs to a firm when that firm's nearest depot is strictly nearer, by walking, than the other firm's. A tie, or a cell no depot can reach, belongs to neither. A street cell that only one firm's depots can reach belongs to that firm. Return `[a, b]`, the numbers of street cells belonging to each firm.

Write `depot_shares(grid)`.

Example. In `['A..B']` the left street cell is 1 step from `A` and 2 from `B`, and the right one the other way round. The answer is `[1, 1]`.
constraints: At most $300$ rows and $300$ columns; there may be any number of depots of each firm, or none.
$O(\text{rows} \times \text{cols})$ time is the target. A search from each depot in turn is too slow when there are many depots.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Run one breadth-first search that starts from every `A` depot at once, and another from every `B` depot. Then compare the two distances in each street cell.

examples.note: Each street cell is nearer to the depot beside it.
`A` is nearer for the two cells beside it. `B` is nearer for the other three, the middle cell included at 1 step against 2.
Only `A` can reach the first street cell, so it is `A`'s. Nothing reaches the last one.

tests.call: depot_shares([''.join('A' if (i * 300 + j) % 997 == 0 else 'B' if (i * 300 + j) % 991 == 5 else '.' for j in range(300)) for i in range(300)])
depot_shares([''.join('#' if (i * 13 + j * 7) % 11 == 0 else 'A' if (i * 300 + j) % 499 == 3 else 'B' if (i * 300 + j) % 503 == 7 else '.' for j in range(300)) for i in range(300)])
depot_shares([''.join('A' if j == 0 and i % 2 == 0 else 'B' if j == 299 and i % 2 == 1 else '#' if j == 150 and i != 150 else '.' for j in range(300)) for i in range(300)])

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The obvious method runs a breadth-first search from each depot in turn and keeps the smallest distance. That is one full search per depot, which runs out of time when the map holds hundreds of them. The step to the target is a search that starts from every depot of a firm at once, so each firm costs one search.
notes: A search seeded with all of one firm's depots at distance 0 gives every cell its distance to that firm's nearest depot.
Keeping the two firms' distances apart is what lets a tie be seen; one shared search hands each tie to whichever depot was queued first.
Two searches and one comparison pass make the work $O(\text{rows} \times \text{cols})$, however many depots there are.

planted.slip: One shared search hands each tied cell to whichever depot reached it first, instead of to neither.
Letting the search walk through buildings measures straight-line steps, not walking distance.
A search from each depot in turn is right but repeats a full search per depot, too slow on the maps with hundreds of depots.
